---
title: "Plan, run, and examine a large study"
description: >
  How to make the treatment, the target, and the event times from start
  dates, count the cells before you see the results, run a long bootstrap
  with a checkpoint, and read the diagnostics of the draws.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
source("_setup.R")
```

::: {.key-points}
Key points

- Use `trop_rollout()` to make the treatment, the target, and the event times
  from the start date of each unit. Give the event times to `trop()` with
  `event_time`.
- With `event_time`, the groups are correct also when the panel has no row
  for some periods.
- Use `trop_cells()` to count the cells of each group before you calculate the
  bootstrap. It does not show the effects.
- Give all sets of groups to one call of `trop_effects()`. Then the C code
  calculates the estimator only one time for each draw.
- Use `checkpoint` to save the draws to a file during a long run. If R stops,
  the same call continues from the file.
- Read the column `n_draws` and the diagnostics of the draws before you
  report a result.
:::

## A practice rollout

In this practice panel, 60 units have 14 monthly periods. Twenty-four units
start the treatment in month 7, 9, or 11. The other units do not start in the
panel. The units know their start month. Thus, the outcome changes by 0.5 one
month before the start. The true effect is 1 at the start, and it increases by
0.2 each month after the start.

```{r data}
library(fasttrop)
set.seed(42)
units <- sprintf("org%02d", 1:60)
start_month <- c(rep(c(7, 9, 11), each = 8), rep(NA, 36))
panel <- expand.grid(unit = units, month = 1:14, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
panel$start <- start_month[match(panel$unit, units)]
k <- panel$month - panel$start
panel$y <- rnorm(60)[match(panel$unit, units)] + cumsum(rnorm(14, 0, 0.3))[panel$month] +
  rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.3) +
  ifelse(!is.na(k) & k >= 0, 1 + 0.2 * k, 0) + ifelse(!is.na(k) & k == -1, 0.5, 0)
```

## Make the treatment, the target, and the event times

The month before the start is not a good control, because the outcome
changes in that month. `trop_rollout()` marks this month as treated with
`anticipation = 1`. A treated cell is not a control for any fit.

The target is the set of treated cells in the estimate. This study
examines the first 4 months of the treatment. Thus, the window is the event
times 0 to 3. The anticipation month is treated, but it is not in the target.

The event time is the number of months since the true start. Thus, the
anticipation month has the event time -1.

```{r rollout}
r <- trop_rollout(panel$unit, panel$month, panel$start, anticipation = 1,
                  window = c(0, 3))
panel <- cbind(panel, r)
panel[panel$unit == "org01", c("month", "start", "treated", "target", "event_time")]
```

## Fit one time without the bootstrap

The fit uses fixed tuning parameters to keep the build of this page fast. In
a real study, select them with cross-validation before you examine the treated
outcomes. Use `se = "none"`, because the bootstrap comes later with all the
groups.

The argument `event_time` keeps the event times of `trop_rollout()` in the
fit. Then `trop_effects()` and `trop_cells()` use them for the groups.

```{r fit, warning = FALSE}
lambda <- c(time = 0.2, unit = 0.5, nn = 1)
fit <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "treated", unit = "unit",
            time = "month", target = "target", event_time = "event_time",
            lambda = lambda, se = "none")
fit
```

## Count the cells before you see the results

`trop_cells()` shows the cells of each group, but not the effects. Use it to
make sure that the estimate contains the correct cells for your question.

```{r cells}
trop_cells(fit)
```

Each row is an event time. The column `n_cells` counts the cells in the
estimate. The column `n_excluded` counts the treated cells outside of the
target. Event time -1 is the anticipation month. Its cells are treated, but
they are not in the estimate. The column `share` gives the weight of each
event time in the overall estimate.

## Why the fit must keep the event times

A fit without `event_time` finds the start of each run from the treatment.
In this panel, the first treated month is the anticipation month. Thus, all
labels move by one month:

```{r cells-wrong, warning = FALSE}
fit_w <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "treated", unit = "unit",
              time = "month", target = "target", lambda = lambda, se = "none")
head(trop_cells(fit_w), 3)
```

With `anticipation = 1`, `trop_cells()` and `trop_effects()` move the labels
back by one month. This method works only if the panel has a row for the
first treated month of each unit. In the next panel, unit `org01` has no row
for month 6. Month 6 is its anticipation month and its first treated month.
Thus, its first treated row is its true start.

```{r gap, warning = TRUE}
gap <- panel[!(panel$unit == "org01" & panel$month == 6), ]
fit_gap <- trop(gap, outcome = "y", treatment = "treated", unit = "unit",
                time = "month", target = "target", lambda = lambda, se = "none")
```

The first message tells you that the start of the treatment of `org01` is not
certain. The second message is about the design, and it is also true for the
first fit. With `anticipation = 1`, event time -1 now has a cell in the
estimate. This cell is the true start of `org01`:

```{r gap-wrong}
head(trop_cells(fit_gap, anticipation = 1), 3)
```

With `event_time`, the groups are correct. A month without a row does not
change the event times of the other months.

```{r gap-right, warning = FALSE}
fit_gap <- trop(gap, outcome = "y", treatment = "treated", unit = "unit",
                time = "month", target = "target", event_time = "event_time",
                lambda = lambda, se = "none")
head(trop_cells(fit_gap), 3)
```

A month without a row in the middle of a treatment run does not stop the run.
`trop()` gives such a cell the treatment of the rows before and after it. The
cell has no outcome. Thus, it is not in the estimate, and the labels of the
other months do not change, also with `anticipation`.

## Choose the weights

By default, each cell has the same weight. Thus, a unit with more cells in a
group has more weight in that group. With `weights = "unit"`, each unit has
the same total weight in each group. In this study, each treated unit has 4
cells in the window. Thus, the two rules give the same estimates here.

With `unit_weights`, each unit gets its own weight, for example its number of
workers before the treatment. Use a value that the treatment cannot change.
A unit with a weight of 0 is not in the estimate. The weights are relative.
Thus, only the ratios of the weights change the estimate.

```{r weights}
workers <- setNames(round(runif(60, 50, 500)), units)
trop_cells(fit, by = "overall", weights = "unit", unit_weights = workers)
```

## Run the bootstrap one time for all groups

Make the bootstrap rows one time with `trop_boot_rows()`. Then give all sets
of groups to one call of `trop_effects()` as a named list. Each draw then
calculates the estimator only one time, for all the groups.

A long bootstrap can take hours. With `checkpoint`, the function saves the
draws to a file after each block of draws. With `progress = TRUE`, it shows
the number of draws that are done and an estimate of the time that is left.
This page uses 100 draws. A real study must use more draws.

```{r boot, message = TRUE}
W <- tapply(panel$treated, list(panel$unit, panel$month), sum)
rows <- trop_boot_rows(W, n_boot = 100, seed = 7)
ck <- tempfile("my-study-draws-", fileext = ".rds")
res <- trop_effects(fit, by = list(att = "overall", event = "event_time",
                                   cohort = "cohort"),
                    boot_rows = rows, checkpoint = ck, progress = TRUE)
res$event
```

If R stops before the end, run the same call again. The function reads the
file and calculates only the draws that are not in it. The results are equal
to the results of one run without a stop. The file has a fingerprint of the
calculation. If you change the data, the groups, the weights, the rows, or the
tuning parameters, the function stops with an error. It does not use the old
draws.

## Read the diagnostics

The column `n_draws` gives the number of draws with a value for each group. A
group has no value in a draw if the draw has no treated cell of the group.
The band uses only the draws with a value for all groups. The last lines of
the print show this number.

Many draws can have no value for a group, for example for a small cohort.
Then you can make the draws with the cohort of each unit as `strata` in
`trop_boot_rows()`. The units that are never treated must have their own
stratum, because `strata` cannot have `NA` values. Each draw then has the same
number of units of each cohort as the data:

```{r strata}
first <- tapply(panel$start, panel$unit, function(s) s[1])
cohort <- ifelse(is.na(first), "never", first)
rows_c <- trop_boot_rows(W, n_boot = 100, strata = cohort, seed = 7)
table(cohort[rows_c[1, ]])
```

A group can still have no value in a draw if the untreated units of the draw
do not identify its cells. Thus, examine `n_draws` and the column `n_dropped`
of the diagnostics also with these draws. A cohort with few units has little
variation in such draws.

The attribute `diagnostics` counts the fits of each draw. A fit that does not
converge stops at the iteration limit. A fit that fails has no result,
because the singular value decomposition failed or the result is not finite.

```{r diag}
head(attr(res$event, "diagnostics"), 3)
```

The next fit uses a very low iteration limit to show the messages. Do not use
such a limit in a real study.

```{r diag-low, warning = TRUE}
low <- fit
low$control <- trop_control(max_iter = 1, max_inner = 1)
trop_effects(low, by = "overall", boot_rows = rows[1:10, ])
```

If a draw has fits that did not converge, use a larger `max_iter` in
`trop_control()`. If a draw cannot identify some cells, the draw uses fewer
cells than the estimate. Then the standard error is not the standard error of
the same estimand. Find the reason before you report the result.

## Combine the groups

`coef()` and `vcov()` give the estimates and their covariance from the draws.
`trop_contrast()` calculates linear combinations of the estimates from the
same draws. It does not calculate the estimator again.

```{r contrast}
ct <- trop_contrast(res$event, list(
  mean_0_3 = c("0" = 1, "1" = 1, "2" = 1, "3" = 1) / 4,
  change_0_to_3 = c("3" = 1, "0" = -1)
))
ct
```

The result is a `trop_effects` object. Thus, `trop_stepdown()` can adjust the
p-values of all the tests in a family together.

```{r stepdown}
trop_stepdown(list(event = res$event, contrast = ct))
```

## Placebo periods for a sensitivity analysis

The 'HonestDiD' package gives confidence sets when parallel trends is not
exactly true. It uses event-time estimates before and after the start, relative
to a reference period. To get estimates before the start, mark these periods
as treated and keep them in the target. Then the fit estimates them as
placebo effects.

In the next fit, the 3 months before the start are placebo periods. The
window starts at event time -3. The event times do not change, because they
count the months from the true start.

```{r placebo, warning = FALSE}
rp <- trop_rollout(panel$unit, panel$month, panel$start, anticipation = 3,
                   window = c(-3, 3))
panel$placebo <- rp$treated
panel$placebo_target <- rp$target
fit_p <- trop(panel, outcome = "y", treatment = "placebo", unit = "unit",
              time = "month", target = "placebo_target", event_time = "event_time",
              lambda = lambda, boot_rows = rows)
ev_p <- trop_effects(fit_p, by = "event_time")
ev_p[, c("event_time", "estimate", "std.error", "n_draws")]
```

The estimate at event time -1 is not near 0, because the units change one
month before the start. In this design, the placebo months are not controls.
Thus, the effects after the start are different from the effects of the first
fit.

`trop_honest_inputs()` subtracts the estimate of the reference period from the
other estimates. It also gives their covariance from the draws. The element
`l_vec` gives the weight of each event time after the reference in the
result of 'HonestDiD'.

```{r honest}
inp <- trop_honest_inputs(ev_p, reference = -2)
round(inp$betahat, 3)
c(pre = inp$numPrePeriods, post = inp$numPostPeriods)
inp$l_vec
```

With the reference -2, event time -1 is a period after the reference. Thus,
the sensitivity analysis treats the anticipation month as a treated period.
By default, 'HonestDiD' examines the first period after the reference. Here,
this period is event time -1. Give `l_vec` to examine event time 0. With
`event_times = 0:3`, `l_vec` gives the mean of the event times 0 to 3.

The next code gives the inputs to 'HonestDiD'. This website does not run this
code, because it does not install 'HonestDiD'.

```{r honest-run, eval = FALSE}
HonestDiD::createSensitivityResults_relativeMagnitudes(
  betahat = inp$betahat, sigma = inp$sigma,
  numPrePeriods = inp$numPrePeriods, numPostPeriods = inp$numPostPeriods,
  l_vec = inp$l_vec, Mbarvec = c(0.5, 1, 2)
)
```

::: {.limit-box}
Limits

- `trop_cells()` counts cells. It cannot tell you if the estimand answers
  your question. Write the estimand before you see the results.
- Without `event_time`, the groups use the first treated row of each run.
  If the panel has no row for the first treated period of a run, the event
  times and the cohort of that run are wrong. `trop()` gives a warning when
  the start of a run is not certain.
- The bootstrap keeps the tuning parameters fixed.
- A checkpoint file contains the draws, but not the panel. Keep it in a
  folder on your computer. Do not change the calculation between two runs with
  the same file.
- `trop_honest_inputs()` does not accept event times with gaps. 'HonestDiD'
  treats the estimates as consecutive periods.
- The placebo design changes the fit, because the placebo periods are not
  controls.
:::
